components.text: Whether the multiple appearance claims constitute historically accessible and reliable testimony rather than merely reported claims.
Whether the Pauline bedrock material provides direct sources for all of the named appearance experiences.
Whether the reported multiple appearances constitute sufficiently direct and reliable historical testimony.
Whether calling the early Christian reports bedrock adequately accounts for ordinary source criticism and comparative testimony.
Whether the proposed testimonial criteria are applied consistently to comparable Christian and non-Christian appearance claims.
Whether calling selected Christian sources bedrock improperly privileges sources that support the affirmative conclusion.
Whether agreement with Christian sources can substitute for impartial historical evaluation of their reliability.
Whether appearance testimony satisfies the same reliability standards applied to comparable non-Christian sources.
Whether an unexpected resurrection claim requires an actual resurrection rather than experiences interpreted and socially transmitted afterward.
Whether the reported multiplicity discloses independent experiences or later claims spreading after initial perceived appearances.
Whether an unexpected resurrection claim requires an actual resurrection rather than interpreted experiences and later claims.
Whether reported appearances can originate in sincere perceived experiences without verifying the reality of the perceived object.
Whether Jewish conceptual resources could convert a perceived postmortem sighting into a bodily-resurrection claim.
Whether interpretation of perceived appearances depends on the followers' prior embodied-afterlife framework.
Whether Jewish conceptual resources could convert a perceived postmortem encounter into a bodily-resurrection conclusion.
Whether appearance experiences themselves distinguish bodily resurrection from culturally shaped interpretation.
Whether Jewish embodied-afterlife categories naturally explain the unprecedented claim that one person had risen before the final resurrection.
Whether perceived sightings plus Jewish categories adequately explain the timing and specific content of the immediate claim.
Whether general embodied-afterlife categories explain the innovative claim that Jesus had already risen bodily.
Whether interpreted experiences and communal claims sufficiently explain the timing and individual form of the resurrection belief.
Whether the appearance reports reveal what the alleged witnesses experienced well enough to establish resurrection over ordinary options.
Whether the early source base contains first-person descriptions sufficient to identify the appearances' cause.
Whether a novel interpretation resolves the underlying uncertainty about what was actually perceived.
Whether the appearance reports reveal sufficiently specific experiences to discriminate resurrection from ordinary alternatives.
Whether the unexpected interpretation identifies what occurred rather than merely recording what followers concluded.
Whether familiar postmortem or projected-apparition explanations plausibly cover Paul's hostile pre-conversion situation.
Whether the proposed natural pathway supplies a specific mechanism for Paul's experience and conversion.
Whether an ordinary vision account readily covers an alleged enemy of the deceased person's movement.
Whether Paul's prior hostility materially weakens the proposed perceived-sighting pathway.
Whether difficulty explaining Paul's experience makes resurrection the most probable historical explanation.
Whether testimony from Paul and Peter overcomes the prior improbability associated with an unprecedented physical event.
Whether the claim's singular novelty supports rather than reduces its historical probability.
Whether difficulty specifying Paul's ordinary experience makes resurrection the historically most probable explanation.
Whether limited appearance testimony overcomes the prior evidential weight of consistently observed physical regularities.
Whether an innovative conclusion can establish a physically unprecedented event as historically probable.
Whether appearance evidence must independently make resurrection most probable or may contribute within a broader cumulative explanation.
Whether consistency with resurrection supplies positive evidential weight despite underdetermination by appearances alone.
Whether appearance evidence must independently establish resurrection rather than contribute to a cumulative inference.
Whether evidence consistent with resurrection retains some cumulative relevance despite underdetermination in isolation.
Whether the singularity of the alleged resurrection lacks correspondingly singular historical context that could affect its assessment.
Whether later worldwide worship supplies information capable of resolving the early appearance evidence's underdetermination.
Whether worldwide worship supplies evidence capable of overcoming the historical prior against physical resurrection.
Whether later influence identifies what the earliest alleged witnesses experienced.
Whether widespread conviction and worship establish the truth or miraculous cause of the resurrection claim.
Whether adding later conviction to a cumulative case supplies an independent bridge to the alleged miracle.
Whether widespread conviction and worship establish the truth of the resurrection miracle that produced them.
Whether later conviction supplies an independent causal line rather than merely recording acceptance of the claim.
Whether exceptional Christian scale or growth identifies a miraculous beginning rather than reproducible movement dynamics.
Whether movement growth supplies an independent cumulative evidential line for resurrection.
Whether exceptional Christian expansion and adherence uniquely indicate a miraculous beginning.
Whether growth adds independent diagnostic force to the cumulative resurrection case.
Whether dreams and visions establish the reality of Jesus as their object rather than merely the occurrence of experiences.
Whether recurring religious experiences identify continuing direction of a worldwide mission.
Whether comparable religious vision and healing traditions undermine claimed Christian uniqueness.
Whether later dreams and visions establish the reality and continuing activity of their perceived object.
Whether cross-cultural religious experience uniquely corroborates fulfillment through the activity of the risen Jesus.
Whether Christian vision reports differ because people outside Christianity see Jesus and move across religious boundaries.
Whether ordinary social reinforcement explains reports arising among people initially outside Christian communities.
Whether the asserted cross-religious pattern has been established under impartial source standards.
Whether the relevant Jesus reports differ from ordinary visions occurring within a person's existing religious tradition.
Whether conversion across religious boundaries supplies a distinction beyond the mere growth of a successful movement.
